beats.headline: Why does Java load classes lazily?
beats.subline: It isn't just for speed. It's a security requirement for the entire runtime.
beats.narration: Java doesn't load every class at startup. It uses a lazy, hierarchical loading system. If you've ever wondered why your app crashes with a LinkageError, it's usually because this delegation model got tangled.

beats.title: The ClassLoader Hierarchy
beats.subtitle: Parent Delegation ensures security
beats.narration: The hierarchy is strict. When a class is requested, the loader delegates upward to the Bootstrap loader first. This prevents third-party code from injecting fake versions of core JDK classes like String.

beats.title: Inspecting the Chain

steps.explanation: getParent() traverses the hierarchy. Bootstrap returns null because it is implemented in native C++.
A class's identity is the pair: (Fully Qualified Name, Defining ClassLoader).

beats.narration: You can inspect this chain yourself. Remember: a class's identity is defined by its name AND its ClassLoader. If two loaders define the same class, they are completely incompatible types.

beats.title: Linking: Preparation vs. Init

top.label: Preparation
points: Sets fields to default zero values (0, null)

bottom.label: Initialization
points: Assigns actual values defined in code

beats.narration: Linking is subtle. During Preparation, the JVM sets static fields to zero. The actual assignment to 42 only happens later during Initialization, when the class is first actively used.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Preparation sets zeros; Init runs logic

beats.narration: That's the loading phase. In Part 2, we map out the JVM memory areas, including why Metaspace replaced PermGen.

beats.headline: Where do your variables actually reside?
beats.subline: The JVM isn't just one big blob of memory. It's a precise map of shared and private areas.
beats.narration: Stop guessing where your objects live. The JVM splits memory into thread-shared areas and thread-private stacks. Understanding this is the only way to debug StackOverflowErrors and memory leaks.

beats.title: JVM Memory Layout
beats.subtitle: Shared vs. Thread-Private
beats.narration: The Heap holds your objects. Metaspace stores class metadata in native memory—not the heap. Each thread gets its own private Stack for method frames, which is why recursion depth is limited.

beats.title: Inside a Stack Frame

steps.explanation: LIFO workspace where bytecode pushes values to perform arithmetic.

beats.narration: Every method call pushes a Frame. Inside, the Local Variable Table holds your variables, while the Operand Stack acts as a LIFO workspace for calculations. It's a stack-based machine, not register-based.

beats.title: PermGen vs. Metaspace

top.label: PermGen (Java 7)
points: Hard to size, prone to OOM

beats.narration: Java 8 killed PermGen. Metaspace now lives in native memory. It grows dynamically, but you should still set a cap to prevent runaway native memory usage from killing your OS process.

beats.narration: Memory management is clear. In Part 3, we look at the Execution Engine: how the JIT compiler turns your bytecode into lightning-fast native machine code.

beats.headline: Why is Java so fast?
beats.subline: It's not just bytecode. It's the JIT compiler profiling your code while it runs.
beats.narration: Java starts as interpreted bytecode, but it doesn't stay that way. The JIT compiler watches your code, profiles the hot paths, and compiles them into native CPU instructions on the fly.

beats.title: Tiered Compilation Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From Interpreter to Native
beats.narration: The JVM uses tiered compilation. Tier 0 interprets code. Tiers 1 to 3 use C1 for fast native code. Finally, Tier 4 uses C2 for aggressive, profile-guided optimizations based on real usage.

beats.title: C2 Optimization: Inlining

steps.explanation: C2 copies the body of add() directly into totalPrice(), removing the method call overhead.

beats.narration: C2 is brilliant at inlining. By pulling the logic of small methods directly into the caller, it eliminates call frames and opens the door for constant folding and dead-code elimination.

beats.title: Escape Analysis

bottom.label: Scalar Replacement
bottom.code: int px = x; int py = y;

beats.narration: If C2 proves an object doesn't escape the method, it performs scalar replacement. It tears the object apart and keeps fields in registers. No heap allocation, no GC. Pure speed.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Tiered compilation balances startup vs speed
beats.narration: JIT is the secret sauce. In Part 4, we cover what happens when those speculative optimizations go wrong and how the JVM safely deoptimizes code.

beats.headline: What if the JIT compiler guesses wrong?
beats.subline: The JVM is speculative. It optimizes for the common case and handles the rare case by throwing it away.
beats.narration: The JIT compiler makes assumptions. If those assumptions are violated—like a new class being loaded—the JVM must perform a deoptimization. It's a complex dance that keeps your app running safely.

beats.title: The Deoptimization Cycle
beats.subtitle: Safepoints ensure consistency
beats.narration: When a speculative optimization fails, the JVM reaches a safepoint. It halts the thread, discards the optimized code, and reverts to the interpreter. It's slow, but it's correct.

beats.title: Monitoring Compilation
beats.caption: Watch the tiers in action
beats.narration: Use the PrintCompilation flag to see the JVM promoting methods through tiers. You'll see methods move from Tier 1 to Tier 4 as they get hotter. It's the best way to visualize JIT behavior.

beats.title: Speculation vs. Reality
beats.narration: C2 assumes your code stays consistent. If you suddenly introduce a new implementation, the guard check fails. The JVM deoptimizes, updates its profile, and recompiles. It's adaptive, not static.
